blocks.text: Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) has several core concepts that make programs organized, reusable, and easier to manage. These concepts include classes and objects, encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.

blocks.title: Do You Know?
blocks.text: A class is like a blueprint, while an object is the real thing created from that blueprint.
Classes and Objects – Representing Real-World Entities in Code

A class is a blueprint or template that defines the properties (attributes) and actions (methods) of an entity. An object is an instance of a class that holds actual values for its attributes (as shown in Figure 3.1). Classes and objects allow programmers to model real-world entities in code. Using classes and objects helps organize data and related functionality together, making programs more structured.

blocks.alt: Class and object diagram: a box Class: Person lists Attributes (name, age, gender) and Methods (eat(), sleep(), work()) beside a person silhouette. Arrows lead to Object P1 (name = Bob, age = 34, gender = Male; eat(), sleep(), work()) with a picture of a man, and Object P2 (name = Jenny, age = 27, gender = Female; eat(), sleep(), work()) with a picture of a woman.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.1: Diagram Showing Class and Object relationship (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.1).

blocks.text: Example

class Student:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def display(self):
        print("Student Name:", self.name)

# Creating objects
object1 = Student("Ali")
object2 = Student("Ahmed")

# Using objects
object1.display()
object2.display()

items: class Student → defines a blueprint for students
__init__ → sets the name when an object is created
object1 and object2 → two different student objects
Each object has its own data (Ali, Ahmed)

blocks.text: Encapsulation
Encapsulation is a concept in Object Oriented Programming (OOP) where we bundle data (variables) and methods (functions) into a single unit (class) and restrict direct access to the data.
Unlike languages like Java or C++, Python does not have strict "private" or "protected" keywords. Instead, it relies on naming conventions to signal how data should be accessed.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Hide the data and control access using methods.
Why Encapsulation is important
Example:
Think of a bank account:
Your balance is hidden
You can only access it using:
You cannot directly change the balance; this is encapsulation.
1. Levels of Access Control
In Python, you can control the visibility of class members using specific naming prefixes:

items: Public Members: These are accessible from anywhere—inside or outside the class. By default, all members in Python are public (as shown in Figure 3.2). Syntax: self.attribute_name

Protected Members: These are intended for internal use within the class and its subclasses. It is a convention (not a restriction) to signal to other developers that the member should not be accessed from outside. Syntax: self._attribute_name (single underscore)

Private Members: These are highly restricted and cannot be easily accessed from outside the class. Python uses a mechanism called Name Mangling to change the internal name of the variable to prevent accidental access. Syntax: self.__attribute_name (double underscore)

A green arrow with a tick, labelled Access allowed, goes to the Public Methods / Interface box (getValue(), setValue()) inside a Class Object box; a dotted arrow leads from the methods to the Private Data box (__private_variable). A red dashed line with a cross, labelled Direct access restricted, runs from the user to the private data.

Inheritance – Reusing and Extending Functionality

Inheritance allows a class to take properties and methods from another class. The new class, called a subclass, can add or modify features of the parent class. Inheritance promotes code reuse and reduces redundancy. It also makes it easier to extend programs without rewriting existing code.
There are the following types of inheritance:

Single Inheritance: Single inheritance occurs when a child class (subclass) inherits attributes and methods from exactly one parent class (superclass). This is the most fundamental form of inheritance in Python, promoting code reusability by allowing the child class to extend or modify the behavior of the parent (as shown in Figure 3.3).

blocks.alt: Single inheritance: a Child Class box below a Parent Class box, joined by a line with a hollow arrowhead at the Parent Class.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.3: Single Inheritance (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.3).

blocks.text: Example:
In this example, the Dog class inherits the basic functionality of an Animal but adds its own specific behavior.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: self is the reference to the current object, passed automatically to instance methods.

items: Parent Class (Base Class): The class whose properties are inherited. In the example above, Animal is the parent class.
Child Class (Derived Class): The class that inherits from the parent. It is defined by passing the parent class name in parentheses: class Child(Parent):.

Method Overriding: A child class can provide a specific implementation of a method that is already provided by its parent. You can use the super() function to call the parent's version of that method.

blocks.text: Multiple Inheritance: Multiple inheritance in Python allows a single class to inherit features (attributes and methods) from more than one parent class. This enables a child class to combine behaviors from different sources, such as a Smartphone class inheriting from both a Camera and a Computer class (as shown in Figure 3.4).

blocks.alt: Multiple inheritance: a Child Class box below two boxes, Parent Class 1 and Parent Class 2; lines from the child go to both parents, each ending in a hollow arrowhead at the parent.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.4: Multiple Inheritance (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.4).

blocks.text: Example:
In this example, the Child class inherits from both Father and Mother classes. It can access methods from both parent classes.

Multilevel Inheritance: Multilevel inheritance in Python occurs when a class inherits from another drived class, creating a chain of inheritance similar to a family tree (Grandparent → Parent → Child). In this structure, the "grandchild" class has access to all methods and attributes from both its immediate parent and its grandparent (as shown in Figure 3.5).

blocks.alt: Multilevel inheritance: three boxes in a column, Grand Parent Class at the top, Parent Class in the middle and Child Class at the bottom; each lower class is joined to the one above by a line with a hollow arrowhead at the upper class.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.5: Multilevel Inheritance (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.5).

blocks.text: Example:
In this example, ElectricCar inherits from Car, which in turn inherits from Vehicle.

Polymorphism

Polymorphism means "many forms". It refers to the ability of an entity (like a function or object) to perform different actions based on the context. Technically, Polymorphism allows the same method, function, or operator to behave differently depending on the object it is working with. This makes code more flexible and reusable.

Example: In a backend payment system, multiple payment options are available, such as Credit Card, UPI, NetBanking, and Wallet. All payment types use a common method named processPayment(), but different implementations:

items: NetBanking Payment: redirects to bank login

blocks.text: The method name remains the same, but the action changes based on the payment type.
Types of Polymorphism
Polymorphism refers to the ability of the same method or operation to behave differently based on object or context. It mainly includes compile-time and runtime polymorphism (as shown in Figure 3.6).

blocks.alt: Polymorphism tree: Polymorphism branches into Compile-time Polymorphism, which leads to Method Overloading, and Runtime Polymorphism, which leads to Method Overriding.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.6: Polymorphism example showing the same function behaving differently (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.6).

blocks.text: 1. Compile-time Polymorphism

Compile-time polymorphism means deciding which method or operation to run during compilation, usually through method or operator overloading. Languages like Java or C++ support this. But python does not support true method overloading based on function signatures like statically typed languages (e.g., Java or C++). Because Python is dynamically typed, a single function can accept arguments of different types, making signature-based overloading unnecessary. Instead, similar behavior can be achieved using default arguments, variable-length arguments (*args, **kwargs), or conditional logic inside the function.
Example: This code demonstrates method overloading using default and variable-length arguments. The multiply() method works with different numbers of inputs, mimicking compile-time polymorphism.

class Calculator:
    def multiply(self, a=1, b=1, *args):
        result = a * b
        for num in args:
            result *= num
        return result

# Create object
calc = Calculator()

# Using default arguments
print(calc.multiply())
print(calc.multiply(4))

# Using multiple arguments
print(calc.multiply(2, 3))
print(calc.multiply(2, 3, 4))
2. Runtime Polymorphism (Overriding)

Runtime polymorphism means that the behavior of a method is decided while program is running, based on the object calling it. This happens through Method Overriding a child class provides its own version of a method already defined in the parent class.

Example: This code shows runtime polymorphism using method overriding. The sound() method is defined in base class Animal and overridden in Dog and Cat. At runtime, the correct method is called based on object's class.

Bark
Meow
Some generic sound
blocks.caption: Output

blocks.text: Here, sound method behaves differently depending on whether object is a Dog, Cat or Animal and this decision happens at runtime. This dynamic nature makes Python particularly powerful for runtime polymorphism.
